summary:
EMBER is an evidence-first web app that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA’s microgravity combustion research for fire safety on human missions. In space, fire doesn’t rise: flames become spheres, smoke behaves differently, and a crew can’t step outside. NASA has decades of results on this, but they are spread across reports, datasets and presentations that are hard to find, compare and understand.
We collected 133 NASA sources from Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) and the Technical Reports Server (NTRS), split them into 3,404 searchable passages, and organized them into 29 investigations, 44 findings and 472 test points. Pick a mission (ISS, Gateway, the lunar surface or Mars) and EMBER re-ranks the evidence for it with a transparent score. Every finding, number and answer links back to the exact NASA page it came from. The Habitat Risk Lens shows how close NASA’s tests came to your cabin’s gravity, oxygen and pressure, and Ask the Flame answers questions only from cited NASA passages, and says so when the data doesn’t cover a question.
This matters because the people designing cabins, materials and fire procedures for the Moon and Mars need fast, trustworthy access to what has actually been tested, and to where the evidence runs out.
details:
• What it does
  • Mission Control:key numbers, the top five insights and a cited evidence digest for the chosen mission. The mission switcher (ISS, Gateway, lunar surface, Mars) re-ranks everything.
  • Experiments:29 NASA investigations, from droplets on the ISS to metre-long fires inside Cygnus (the Saffire flights), with filters and keyword + semantic search over their source documents. Each experiment has a page with findings, conditions tested, test-point data (CSV export) and sources.
  • Insights:44 findings ranked by a visible scoring formula with adjustable weights and a per-card score breakdown. Opening a finding shows its evidence and the NASA source page it came from.
  • Habitat Risk Lens:enter cabin gravity, oxygen, pressure and airflow, and see how close NASA tests came, the nearest test points, a flammability map and the evidence gaps.
  • Ask the Flame:a copilot that answers only from retrieved NASA passages, with a citation after every claim, and declines questions the data doesn’t cover.
  • Compare and Methods:two or three experiments side by side; a methods page with the sources, pipeline, scoring and coverage formulas, and limitations.
  • Bangla (বাংলা):a language toggle switches the key interface text to Bengali; evidence and quotes stay in English so they remain verbatim and traceable.

How it works

  • Collection:investigation records, documents and tables from the public NASA PSI repository API, and reports and presentations from the NTRS API. Every source is listed with its URL, licence and access date.
  • Processing (Python + TypeScript):PDFs are split into page-aware passages (about 350 tokens); experimental tables are normalized into 472 test points with units converted. Candidate findings are drafted from the passages, and a script rejects any quoted excerpt that is not word-for-word in its source passage (excerpts are at most 25 words).
  • Ranking:each finding gets a transparent insight score (severity, actionability, evidence strength and relevance to the chosen mission). The weights are visible and adjustable.
  • Answers:Retrieve (keyword BM25 and semantic embeddings over 3,404 passages, fused, 8 kept) → Gate (if nothing is close enough, decline and name the nearest experiments) → Answer (the model may only use those passages and must cite one after every factual sentence) → Check (citations to anything not retrieved are removed and flagged).
  • Offline mode:without an AI key the site still works, with saved cited answers and verbatim passages.

Benefits

  • Decades of NASA fire research in one place, searchable in seconds and ranked for a specific mission.
  • Every claim traceable to its NASA source page, so users can check it themselves.
  • Honest about limits: AI-drafted findings are labelled, the Risk Lens measures distance to tested conditions rather than predicting outcomes, and the copilot declines when the evidence is silent.
  • Free in any browser, keyboard accessible, with reduced-motion support and a Bengali interface for local reach.

What we hope to achieve

Next, we want domain experts to review and verify the AI-drafted findings, widen the corpus beyond the current 133 sources, and grow EMBER toward an evidence assistant that mission planners, and one day crews on the Moon and Mars, could consult. We also want it to stay open, so students and engineers anywhere, including in Bangladesh, can explore NASA’s fire research.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages:TypeScript, Python 3.11
  • Web app:Next.js 16 (App Router), React, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Magic UI, GSAP, three.js with React Three Fiber, D3, zustand, zod; hosted on Vercel
  • Search and AI:MiniSearch (BM25), transformers.js with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings, Vercel AI SDK with gpt-oss-120b on Groq
  • Data pipeline:PyMuPDF for PDF text extraction, NASA PSI and NTRS APIs
  • Quality:Vitest, Playwright end-to-end tests with axe-core accessibility checks
  • Demo video:HyperFrames (HTML to video), GSAP, three.js, FFmpeg, Kokoro text-to-speech
  • Hardware:none; it runs in any modern browser

Limitations

All 44 findings are AI drafts awaiting human verification, so rankings may change. The corpus is a curated selection of 133 sources, not all of PSI or NTRS. EMBER is a research exploration tool: it is not an official NASA product and not guidance for operational safety decisions.
